before: One of the most common concerns people have after suffering an injury in a car accident, truck collision, or workplace incident is whether they can afford to hire a lawyer. The contingency fee system removes that barrier entirely. Under this arrangement, your attorney does not charge any fees upfront — instead, the lawyer's payment comes as a percentage of the compensation recovered in your case. If your case does not result in a settlement or verdict, you owe nothing for legal representation. Cornell Law Institute provides a helpful overview of how contingency fees operate in the American legal system.

Contingency fee percentages in personal injury cases typically range from 33.3% to 40% of the recovery, depending on several factors:

Stage of CaseTypical Fee RangeExplanation
Pre-litigation settlement33.3% (one-third)Case settles before a lawsuit is filed

Workers' compensation fees follow separate rules: in Georgia they need State Board of Workers' Compensation approval and are capped at 25% (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-108), and in South Carolina they are up to 33.3% with Commission approval (S.C. Code Regs. 67-1205).

before:
Georgia's Rules of Professional Conduct (Georgia Rule 1.5) govern contingency fee arrangements. Key requirements include:

  • Written agreement required: All contingency fee arrangements must be in writing, signed by the client
  • Fee must be reasonable: The fee percentage must be reasonable in light of the complexity, risk, and amount of work involved
  • Prohibited cases: Contingency fees are not permitted in criminal cases or most domestic relations matters
  • Expense disclosure: The agreement must clearly state whether expenses are deducted before or after the fee calculation and what happens to expenses if the case is unsuccessful
  • Statute of limitations: Georgia's 2-year statute of limitations for personal injury claims (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) makes it important to consult an attorney promptly — delaying can forfeit your right to file
  • Comparative fault: Under O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33, your recovery is reduced by your percentage of fault, and you cannot recover if you are 50% or more at fault
after:
Georgia's Rules of Professional Conduct (Georgia Rule 1.5) govern contingency fee arrangements. Key requirements include:

  • Written agreement required: All contingency fee agreements must be in writing and state the percentage(s) for settlement, trial or appeal (Rule 1.5(c)(1))
  • Fee must be reasonable: The fee percentage must be reasonable in light of the complexity, risk, and amount of work involved
  • Prohibited cases: Contingency fees are not permitted in criminal defense cases, or in domestic relations matters when the fee depends on securing a divorce or on the amount of alimony, support or a property settlement
  • Expense disclosure: The agreement must state the litigation and other expenses to be deducted from the recovery and whether they are deducted before or after the fee is calculated
  • Statute of limitations: Georgia's 2-year statute of limitations for personal injury claims (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) makes it important to consult an attorney promptly — delaying can forfeit your right to file
  • Comparative fault: Under O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33, your recovery is reduced by your percentage of fault, and you cannot recover if you are 50% or more at fault

before:
South Carolina's Rules of Professional Conduct (Rule 1.5) impose similar requirements with some differences:

  • Written agreement required: Must include the fee percentage, expense terms, and the client's right to terminate
  • Reasonableness standard: South Carolina courts apply a reasonableness test considering the complexity, amount involved, and customary fees in the locality
  • Prohibited cases: Same restrictions on criminal and most domestic relations cases
  • Client's right to terminate: A client can terminate the contingency fee arrangement at any time, though the attorney may be entitled to compensation for work already performed (quantum meruit)
  • Statute of limitations: South Carolina's 3-year statute of limitations (S.C. Code § 15-3-530) provides more time but should not encourage delay
  • Comparative fault: South Carolina bars recovery only if you are 51% or more at fault — slightly more favorable than Georgia's threshold
after:
South Carolina's Rules of Professional Conduct (Rule 1.5) impose similar requirements with some differences:

  • Written agreement required: Must be signed by the client and state the percentage(s) for settlement, trial or appeal, the expenses to be deducted, whether they come off before or after the fee, and any expenses the client will be expected to pay
  • Reasonableness standard: South Carolina courts apply a reasonableness test considering the complexity, amount involved, and customary fees in the locality
  • Prohibited cases: Same restrictions on criminal and most domestic relations cases
  • Client's right to terminate: A client can terminate the contingency fee arrangement at any time, though the attorney may be entitled to compensation for work already performed (quantum meruit)
  • Statute of limitations: South Carolina's 3-year statute of limitations (S.C. Code § 15-3-530) provides more time but should not encourage delay
  • Comparative fault: South Carolina bars recovery only if you are 51% or more at fault — slightly more favorable than Georgia's threshold

before: Most accident victims cannot afford to pay a lawyer $300-$500 per hour while simultaneously dealing with medical bills, lost wages, and recovery. The contingency fee system ensures that financial resources do not determine who can obtain quality legal representation. Whether your claim involves a slip and fall, medical malpractice, or a wrongful death, the contingency fee system levels the playing field.
after: Most accident victims cannot afford to pay a lawyer by the hour — often hundreds of dollars an hour — while simultaneously dealing with medical bills, lost wages, and recovery. The contingency fee system ensures that financial resources do not determine who can obtain quality legal representation. Whether your claim involves a slip and fall, medical malpractice, or a wrongful death, the contingency fee system levels the playing field.

before: The contingency fee system allows injury victims to hire experienced attorneys with no upfront costs — the lawyer's fee is a percentage of the recovery, typically 33-40%. Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and South Carolina (S.C. Code § 15-3-530) both require written fee agreements. Case expenses like expert witnesses and filing fees are advanced by the firm and deducted from the settlement.
after: The contingency fee system allows injury victims to hire experienced attorneys with no upfront costs — the lawyer's fee is a percentage of the recovery, commonly one-third, often higher if suit is filed or the case is tried. Georgia and South Carolina both require contingent fee agreements to be in writing (Rule 1.5(c) of each state's Rules of Professional Conduct); South Carolina also requires the client's signature. Case expenses like expert witnesses and filing fees are typically advanced by the firm and repaid from the recovery. At Roden Law, fees and costs apply only upon successful recovery — no fees or costs with no recovery.
